Comparison of velocity sedimentation and equilibrium 
sedimentation for the separation of subcellular particles. 
In velocity sedimentation, separation relies on different velocity of 
sedimentation through a shallow sucrose (or other material) 
gradient. The sucrose is added to prevent mixing by convection. 
In equilibrium sedimentation, subcellular particles sediment until 
they reach a zone of solution that matches their density. At 
equilibrium, the organelles distribute themselves over a narrow 
region of the tube corresponding to the density of the organelle. 
The organelles can then be harvested from a narrow band.

The replication fidelity by DNA polymerase
18
• The free energy differences resulting from the changes in hydrogen bonding 
between matched and mismatched bases are large enough to favor the formation 
of correctly matched base pairs by 100-fold. 
• Consequently, base selection determined by hydrogen bonding between 
complementary bases result in an error frequency corresponding to one incorrect 
base incorporation in every 100 nucleotides of new DNA strand. 
• However, the error frequency during DNA replication corresponds to less than 
1/109 nucleotides incorporated and is much lower than would be predicted simply 
on the basis of complementary base pairing.
 The much higher degree of fidelity actually achieved results largely from the 
activities of DNA polymerase.

• DNA polymerase actively discriminates against incorporation of a mismatched 
base by adapting to the conformation of a correct base pair.
• This ability of DNA polymerase to select matched nucleotides for incorporation 
increases the accuracy of replication about a 1000-fold.

its structure are of much greater consequence than are alterations in other cell 
components, such as RNAs or proteins.

replication. In addition, various chemical changes occur in DNA either 
spontaneously or as a result of exposure to chemicals or radiation. 
• To maintain the integrity of their genomes, cells have had to evolve mechanisms 
to repair damaged DNA. 
1) Direct reversal of the chemical reaction responsible for DNA damage 
2) Removal of the damaged bases followed by their replacement with newly 
synthesized DNA

2.3. Mismatch repair

• During DNA replication, mismatched bases are removed by the proofreading 
activity of DNA polymerase.

to identify and excise the mismatched base specifically from the newly 
replicated DNA strand, allowing the error to be corrected and the original 
sequence restored.
• The mismatch repair system distinguishes between parental DNA and newly 
synthesized DNA.

Translesion DNA synthesis
11
• The direct reversal and excision repair systems act to correct DNA damage 
before replication, so that replicative DNA synthesis can proceed using an 
undamaged DNA strand as a template. 
• Cells possess several specialized DNA polymerases that is capable of

= Translesion DNA synthesis
• Translesion DNA synthesis provides an alternative mechanism by which 
the cell can bypass DNA damage at the replication fork, which can then 
be corrected after replication is complete.

Specialized DNA polymerases
13
• Specialized DNA polymerases exhibit low fidelity when copying undamaged DNA 
and lack 3′  5′ proofreading activity.

of DNA damage, although they are “error-prone” in inserting bases opposite 
other forms of damaged DNA or in the synthesis of DNA from a normal 
undamaged template.

• Double-strand breaks are a dangerous form of DNA damage, because the 
continuity of the DNA molecule is disrupted by breaks in both strands.

template strand, or induced by ionizing radiation and some chemicals.
• Because they affect both strands of DNA, double-strand breaks are repaired by 
recombinational repair, which rejoins the broken strands.

– Homologous recombination

Summary and 
Key terms
17
• Direct reversal repair is to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers on the same DNA 
strand by photoreactivation using energy from visible light.
• Base-excision repair is to recognize specific lesions (deamination) and repair at AP 
(apyrimidinic or apurinic) site.

containing the lesion.

• Translesion DNA synthesis repairs lesions by specialized DNA polymerases that are 
capable of replicating DNA across from a site of DNA damage.
• Double-strand breaks are repaired by recombination to rejoin the damaged 
strands, either by nonhomologous end joining of the broken ends or by 
homologous recombination with an undamaged chromosome.

10.2 Protein Folding and Processing

Chaperones and protein folding

Protein folding is facilitated by chaperones

Many polypeptides fold during synthesis and undergo additional processing to become

functional.
Chaperones are proteins that facilitate folding of other proteins
Chaperones bind exposed regions of nascent chains as they emerge from the

ribosome.
They stabilize unfolded intermediates and limit inappropriate aggregation.

Chaperones and protein folding

Action of chaperones during protein transport

Chaperones also stabilize unfolded polypeptide chains during their transport into

organelles
Partially unfolded proteins stabilized by chaperones are transported across the

mitochondrial membrane
Mitochondrial chaperones facilitate transport and subsequent folding of the polypeptide

chain within the organelle

Chaperones and protein folding

Sequential actions of chaperones

Many chaperones were initially identified as heat-shock proteins (Hsp)
Chaperones of the Hsp70 family bind to and stabilize unfolded polypeptide chains

during translation
Some substrates subsequently enter a chaperonin for assisted folding.
Hsp70 uses an ATPase cycle: hydrolysis stabilizes binding; nucleotide exchange and
